public.prompt: Read the profiler/process/timing records. Judge the dominant-stage diagnosis and whether the isolated-change conclusion is supported. The same completed-example count and training computation apply in both runs. Classify every supplied excerpt; judge the criterion named in that excerpt.

items.text:
```python
with torch.profiler.profile(...) as prof:
    with record_function("loading"): batch = next(loader)
    with record_function("transfer"): batch = move_batch(batch)
    with record_function("model"): bounded_training_step(batch)
print(prof.key_averages().table(...))
```
Labeled-region elapsed attribution (seconds): {"loading": 8.0, "transfer": 1.0, "model": 1.0}. Same-window docker stats: CPU busy during loading, memory below fixed limit; docker top: intended loader/training processes present. Reproduction shows waiting for loading between model regions. One supported loading factor changes; transfer and model stay fixed. Warm-up occurs in both runs. Final timings exclude profiler overhead and synchronize CUDA before and after the measured workload: 10.0 seconds before, 6.0 after. Review concludes loading is dominant and the isolated change improves this bounded workload.
Loading dominates the labeled trace, but the reviewer changes both model width and loading configuration and attributes any improvement only to loading.
CUDA timing uses unsynchronized CPU timestamps and excludes waiting for the accelerator to finish.
The reference timing is profiled and includes first-call setup; the modified timing is warmed-up and unprofiled.
docker stats reports high CPU use; no region table or trace is inspected, yet the report identifies model computation rather than loading as the dominant stage.

i1.message: Labeled attribution and supporting process evidence identify loading; the matched unprofiled, warmed-up and synchronized rerun measures an actual improvement.

i2.message: Two changes and a different model computation do not isolate the supported loading factor.

i3.message: Asynchronous work may complete outside these timings.

i4.message: The unequal overhead and warm-up scopes confound the final comparison.

i5.message: Resource use alone does not attribute the limiting stage; profiler labels or trace evidence are needed.

steps.title: Choose CPU or GPU capacity for a bounded training workload

blocks.text: Compare CPU and accelerator options on matched work, quality, memory and billing scope, not utilization alone.

Check accelerator availability and place the model and minibatches on the selected device. Benchmark the same bounded workload and quality requirements, retaining the declared treatment of data movement and warm-up. Running VMs incur compute billing; stopping compute can leave persistent-disk and other charges.

Estimate compute execution cost using measured runtime and the supplied rate, with its billing scope. For authorized supplied VMs only, use gcloud compute instances start INSTANCE --zone=ZONE or stop INSTANCE --zone=ZONE; wait and inspect the resulting state. Connect to a running authorized VM with gcloud compute ssh INSTANCE --zone=ZONE.

steps.title: CPU versus accelerator: runtime and lifecycle cost

blocks.text: Compare the registered CPU and accelerator records under the same workload, quality and memory limits. Execution cost uses the supplied rate and bounded execution duration; billing interpretation also needs lifecycle duration. Retain the declared movement and warm-up scope. Start, connect to and inspect only authorized instances; stop both after measurement and verify the result. A faster option can still cost more, and persistent-disk or other charges can remain after compute stops.
Faster is not automatically cheaper or eligible. Stopping compute does not end every charge; preserve billing scope.

public.prompt:
Read the comparable CPU/accelerator measurements and lifecycle decisions. Both meet the fixed completion, quality, memory and execution-time limits; the capacity rule selects the lower lifecycle compute cost among eligible options. Measurements include declared movement and warm-up scopes.
```text
option | model_device | feature_device | target_device | completed | task_quality_requirement_met | observed_memory_bytes | memory_limit_bytes | execution_seconds | lifecycle_seconds | rate_per_second | execution_compute_cost | lifecycle_compute_cost | billing_scope | stopped_state_verified | final_instance_state | remaining_charge_note
CPU | cpu | cpu | cpu | True | True | 24000 | 30000 | 60.0 | 90 | 0.01 | 0.6 | 0.9 | currency units per second; simplified compute-only rate | True | TERMINATED | persistent disk and other charges may remain
accelerator | cuda | cuda | cuda | True | True | 28000 | 30000 | 20.0 | 50 | 0.04 | 0.8 | 2.0 | currency units per second; simplified compute-only rate | True | TERMINATED | persistent disk and other charges may remain
``` Classify every supplied excerpt; judge the criterion named in that excerpt.

items.text: Authorized lifecycle review: describe identity/initial stopped state for each option; start, wait and describe running state; SSH to each authorized running VM; execute the same bounded matrix task with all operands on the selected available device. Stop both afterward, wait and describe each final stopped state. Keep both duration/rate records. Execution cost uses execution_seconds × rate; lifecycle compute cost uses lifecycle_seconds × rate. The review selects CPU under the stated capacity rule and retains the continuing-disk/other-charge note.
The accelerator executes faster, so the reviewer selects it without checking lifecycle cost under the stated lower-cost rule.
Both stop commands are issued, but only the CPU instance is described afterward; the accelerator state is assumed.
The reviewer records execution_seconds × rate as lifecycle billing and deletes the continuing-charge note.

i1.message: Comparable completion, quality, memory and time are checked before lifecycle cost; both states are verified and execution cost is kept distinct from billing scope.

i2.message: Faster execution is not necessarily lower lifecycle cost; the supplied rule compares eligible lifecycle compute costs.

i3.message: Both resulting stopped states require inspection and verification.

i4.message: Execution and lifecycle durations differ, and stopping compute can leave disk or other charges.

blocks.text: Wrap the measured computation in the PyTorch profiler context and mark data-loading and model-computation regions with record_function labels.
Inspect key_averages().table(...) or the trace to attribute elapsed operator and labeled-region work to the observed bottleneck.
Change one supported bottleneck factor and compare the same bounded workload again rather than inferring improvement only from a code change.

Inspect CPU and memory measurements and running process state during the profiled interval, using docker stats and docker top for a containerized run, to distinguish resource limits from stage timing evidence.
For the same supplied task: A trace attributes work; final unprofiled timing tests improvement.

For s05 item i3, CPU timestamps around asynchronous CUDA calls need torch.cuda.synchronize() immediately before starting the clock and before stopping it, so the duration includes completed accelerator work. For item i4, warm up both versions and measure the same workload without the profiler in both final timing runs. Do not compare a profiled first-call reference with a warmed-up unprofiled modified run. Keep these timing controls separate from the profiler trace used for attribution.
